prize_parts.citation: For a visionary, densely patterned body of work in Romanian, above all the novels Blinding and Solenoid, that builds memory, the body and dream into a metaphysical architecture, with poetry as its lyric ground.

statement.case_for: My laureate choice is unchanged: Cărtărescu, alone. The reasons are the work and not the shared first place in round 1, which the chair rightly says is a provisional convergence on shared public knowledge and may reflect correlated assumptions. The voice is distinctive. As publicly described, Blinding (the first volume of the Orbitor trilogy) and Solenoid build very large prose forms in which the intimate, the bodily and the cosmic are one continuing project, and the poetry gives that prose a lyric base. The case rests on more than one book. The prize honours a whole authorship, and a decades-long project of this scale gives the committee several large works to test against each other. That is the sustained-quality evidence I can point to. On the chair's first question, what would count as development rather than recurrence is a change in architecture, not just in motifs: how the book is organised, what governs its large structure, how the narrating consciousness is placed. Solenoid is publicly described as organised differently from the Orbitor volumes, but I have not verified that by close reading and hold it as a claim to be tested. My configuration changes in one respect only. I now scope the citation to the novels, name Blinding and Solenoid, and treat the poetry as ground, not as a co-equal object of the citation. The reason is the thin translation coverage that Carlberg, Palm and Sem-Sandberg raised, and my round-1 wording ('prose and poetry') claimed more than the evidence available to us supports. I rest the case on voice, form, imaginative depth and sustained quality. I do not rest it on Nobel's 'idealist' direction, because that phrase can be stretched to fit almost any serious writer.
statement.case_against: The reservation I cannot remove is that the case depends on density, register and rhythm, and I judge these through translation and public knowledge. If the late digressive volumes mostly restate the earlier ones, the claim of sustained, developing depth weakens, and I cannot rule that out from this record. Sem-Sandberg's standard, that a citation rewards the peaks and overall direction and not uniform quality, is reasonable. But it cannot be applied until someone can say what the peaks are and whether the direction is forward. If close reading or expert reports showed that the peaks are early and the later work circles them, I would give more weight to the written sequences of Zurita or to Tawada. The shortlist descriptions are also brief, and the committee has no verified reading of the originals. A confident whole-oeuvre judgment is therefore not available to me, only a provisional best case among the candidates.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Cărtărescu first but asks whether his scale and recurrent imagery amount to repetition rather than development. She keeps Michon as a serious alternative for concentration of language, and Wright as a serious alternative for reinvention of narrative form.
responses.response: I take the repetition question to be the real test, and I agree no one on this record can settle it. Where I part from you is on what follows if it stays open. You treat it as a reason to keep Michon and Wright in view, and that is fair. For me Michon is still limited by corpus size and by syntax that translation barely carries, so he gives me less to test across a body of work. I do not call his concentration a weakness, but I need more than a few books to judge sustained development, and the committee has not said why a few books suffice. For Wright, I would keep polyphonic voice and structure strictly apart from the political significance of her subject, as you propose. I also share the doubt that a small number of major novels establishes a mature oeuvre. On the repetition question itself, I can only offer a test, not an answer: does Solenoid change what organises the book, or does it re-enter the earlier material in a new frame? If expert reports show the second, I would lower my confidence and say so.

responses.point: Carlberg warns that Nobel's 'idealist' direction is too open an interpretive phrase to carry the case, because it could favour almost any serious writer. She wants the case to rest on voice, form and imaginative depth, and she did not rank Carson because sustained quality is hard to judge across a partly conceptual body of work.
responses.response: I accept the warning. The chair summary places me with Mattson on the idealist point, and if my round-1 text leaned on it, I withdraw that reliance. A phrase that fits everyone cannot discriminate between Cărtărescu and the alternatives, so the citation should say nothing about it and the case should be argued from the work. On Carson, I ranked her third on the strength of formal reinvention of the poetic book, so we differ. I accept your doubt about sustained quality. Her hybrid method is distinctive, but a body of work that is partly scholarship, translation and conceptual form is hard to weigh as a single authorship, and she depends on classical learning that has to be argued rather than assumed. For that reason I do not carry her into my alternatives. She remains an interesting case that I cannot yet verify as sustained major achievement.

responses.point: Palm's round-1 citation names prose and specific works, Blinding and Solenoid, and leaves poetry out. She treats the poetry as secondary context, and she says the committee has not shown why a small corpus like Michon's is enough.
responses.response: Your citation is the better-supported scope, and it is the main reason I have narrowed mine. I had written 'prose and poetry', but the translated coverage of the poetry and the early work is the thinnest part of our knowledge, and a citation should not assert more than the committee can stand behind. I have kept the poetry in as 'lyric ground' so that the citation does not ignore a real part of the authorship, but it is no longer a named object of praise. I also agree with you on Michon: intensity is a real kind of achievement, but whoever argues for it should explain explicitly why a few books are enough. I do not think that explanation has been given. I am not saying it cannot be, and I would listen if Mattson makes it.

responses.point: Olsson, as chair, asks which alternative each member would move to if the repetition concern proved well founded, and on which criteria. He also discloses that his scholarly interest in the fragment, exile and Celan overlaps with Adonis and Tawada, and he names both as alternatives.
responses.response: If the repetition concern proved well founded, I would move first to Zurita (B005) and second to Tawada (B015). For Zurita the grounds are formal and imaginative: a long sequence-based project with an unmistakable voice that turns collective loss into poetic form. The citation would have to rest on the written sequences, Purgatory and Anteparadise, with the landscape and sky-written works as context only. The reservation I would keep is that I know those works mostly by description and cannot judge the Spanish rhythm. For Tawada the grounds are formal invention and range across prose, poetry, essays and drama, but I cannot read Japanese and German equally. A citation would need to name writing across two languages without privileging either, and I would want expert reports on both corpora first. I do not move to Adonis in that case, mainly because of how little of the prosody and allusion I can assess. I appreciate the disclosure about your scholarly overlap. It is useful to know, and it is context and not a finding.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg says the late novel extends the earlier trilogy rather than repeating it. He argues that a citation rewards the oeuvre's peaks and overall direction and does not require uniform quality, and that the citation should credit what survives translation: architecture, imaginative logic and sustained invention.
responses.response: I agree on the wording point: we should credit the architecture and the sustained invention and be modest about sentence-level music. That is another reason to name the novels and keep the poetry as ground. On the standard of peaks and direction, I accept that uniform quality is too high a bar for any long oeuvre, but I would add a condition. Judging by peaks requires knowing what the peaks are and whether the direction is forward, and that is exactly what we cannot show without close reading. Your claim that Solenoid extends the Orbitor project is plausible and I lean toward it, but I treat it as a provisional judgment, not an established fact. I would want the committee to hold the same standard for the alternatives. If expert reports are used for Cărtărescu's late work, they should also be sought for the weaker-covered corpora, so that Cărtărescu is not the only one tested.

uncertainties: I have not independently verified any source and do not claim to have read the full corpus of any candidate. All judgments rest on public knowledge and translation.
Whether Solenoid changes the architecture of the earlier Orbitor project or restates it is unresolved, and no member can settle it from the supplied record.
How much of Cărtărescu's density, register and rhythm survives in translation is unknown, and the citation should credit architecture and invention more than sentence music.
The translated coverage of the poetry and early work is thin. This is why I narrowed the citation to the novels with poetry as context.
For the alternatives, I cannot judge Zurita's Spanish verse rhythm or the weight of his landscape-scale works, and I cannot read Tawada's Japanese and German corpora comparably.
Shared assumptions among members may be correlated, so the convergence on B031 is not independent evidence of merit.
Carlberg's committee voting status is undocumented, and the six-vote, four-vote-majority structure is a modeling assumption.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. It lists professional ties to committee colleagues (Olsson, Mattson, Sem-Sandberg, Palm) and engagement with Swedish Institute, Arts Council and Nordic Council of Ministers programmes. It records no personal, institutional or professional tie to any shortlisted writer. Her translators' seminars and international festival work are context, not a connection to any candidate. Her own practice as a novelist is context only. Her 2021 Femina remarks on women's authorships the Academy had missed are a stated general view and are not applied here as a criterion or as a preference for any candidate. All candidates are assessed on the common literary criteria. Disclosed for transparency, not adjudicated.
